chapter: The Paradise and life in Queens
title: Lapsed dues and befriending union man Clifford Glover
summary: When he let his dues lapse, Clifford Glover calmly explained the benefits over a lunch walk; Nicholas also mentions Walton and Andy Kirk as union officials.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Say a little something about that, any incidents that you remember...

Well I remember, I let my card...my dues lapse and I was...when I went with Timmy Rogers, the union man. That's how Clifford Glover and I at the union became friendly. And he knew I was in...you know it was tough scuffling and I was workin' hard. I guess I just forgot about it, you know, and that was his job at that time to check on all jobs and the cards and who, you know, and he was mad at first, you know, but after he saw me and saw what I was doin' and he got to talk to me and then we became friends, you know what I mean, he explained to me, you know, "You got to keep this up Nick or, you know, you lose all your benefits and all your this and that and the other and your insurance and blah, blah, blah, blah." You know, he brought it on home to me, you know what I mean. But the way he did it was nice, you know. We had lunch one day, he said, "Meet me downtown," and we took a little walk for lunch, we looked in stores and we were talkin' about life and this and that and the other and then we had lunch and then he explained to me, you know. Because he was a political science major at Columbia University. He was a saxophone player before that. Yeah. So that's how we became
friends and so we've been friends ever since. But that little talk and that little walk and that little lunch that day. You know, he opened my eyes, you know.
Did you have other friends in the union, that were officials in the union, that worked...

No, these were my first friends. Oh, no. Walton. He used to be in the pit, the colored man. In the pit. The first colored man in the pit in 1925 playin' trumpet. And we became friendly, yeah. And he's been there...and, of course, Andy Kirk came in later, he's in the union too, yeah.
